title: MKUltra and the Church Committee
bigQuestion: When a government hides what it has done, what does it take for the public to learn the truth, and how much can still be proven?

story.title: The Boxes in the Money Files
story.kicker: In 1977 the CIA finds records of a secret program that were supposed to have been destroyed four years earlier.
paragraphs: It is 1977. A writer named John Marks has asked the CIA, under the Freedom of Information Act, for its records on mind-control research. The agency has an easy answer ready. Its leaders say the key files were destroyed years ago. There is nothing left to give. Still, the law requires a search, so CIA staff go back into the stored records.

The search reaches a place almost no one thought about: the money files. Every secret program still has to pay its bills. Checks go to universities, hospitals and research foundations. Receipts, contracts and payment records get filed by accountants, not by the scientists who ran the work. Those financial files were stored separately. Nobody had included them when the order came to destroy the program's papers.

Box after box, the paperwork is still there. Together the boxes hold about 20,000 documents. They name a program called MKUltra. They show payments for experiments with drugs, including LSD, and with ways to change how people think and behave. Some of the people tested never knew they were part of an experiment.

On 3 August 1977, the new CIA director, Admiral Stansfield Turner, sits before a joint hearing of two Senate committees. He tells senators what the boxes contain. Much of the program had already been exposed by investigators in 1975 and 1976. Now there is more paper. A secret that powerful people tried to erase has been rescued by the dullest records of all: the bills.
story.think: The CIA's leaders tried to destroy MKUltra's records, but the payment files survived. Why might ordinary records like receipts be harder to erase than a program's main files?

lessons.title: Fear in the Early Cold War
lessons.mainIdea: MKUltra began in 1953 because U.S. leaders feared the Soviet Union and its allies had found ways to control people's minds.
reading: In the early 1950s, the United States and the Soviet Union were locked in the *Cold War*. This was a long rivalry between two powers that competed for influence around the world without fighting each other directly. Each side spied on the other. Each side feared the other was about to gain a secret advantage.

The Korean War (1950–1953) added a new fear. Some American prisoners held by North Korea and China signed false confessions or spoke on enemy radio. Newspapers used a new word, *brainwashing*, to describe what might have happened. The idea was that captors could strip away a person's beliefs and put new ones in their place. Researchers later found that harsh treatment, hunger and pressure explained most of it. At the time, though, many officials were alarmed.

CIA leaders asked a question: if the other side could control minds, could the United States learn to do it too, or at least learn to defend against it? On 13 April 1953, CIA Director Allen Dulles approved a program to study the question in secret. It was called MKUltra. The CIA is the *Central Intelligence Agency*, created in 1947 to gather and analyze information about other countries.

Understanding the fear does not excuse what came next. It helps explain it. Historians try to see a decision the way the people inside it saw it, and then judge it by what it did to real people. Both steps matter. Explaining a choice is not the same as approving it.

words.d: the long rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union, from the late 1940s to 1991, fought mostly without direct war between them
a 1950s word for the idea that captors could force a person to give up their beliefs and take on new ones
the U.S. agency, created in 1947, that gathers and analyzes information about other countries; known as the CIA

look.title: Two Ways to Read One Decision
look.text: View A: In 1953, leaders believed the enemy might have a mind-control weapon. They felt they had to study it fast and in secret to protect the country. View B: Fear does not give anyone the right to test drugs on people who have not agreed. A good goal cannot make a harmful method acceptable.
look.prompt: Explain how a historian can take View A seriously as an explanation while still using View B to judge what happened.

check.q: What fear helped lead to MKUltra?
choices: That the Soviet Union and its allies could control people's minds
That the Korean War would reach American cities
That the CIA would be closed down by Congress
That LSD was being sold in American schools
check.why: Reports of 'brainwashing' during the Korean War made officials fear the other side had a way to control minds.

check.q: Who approved MKUltra on 13 April 1953?
choices: President Gerald Ford
Admiral Stansfield Turner
CIA Director Allen Dulles
Senator Frank Church
check.why: Allen Dulles, then director of the CIA, approved the program in April 1953.

check.q: According to the reading, what did later researchers find explained most 'brainwashing' of prisoners?
choices: A secret drug given in their food
Hypnosis done over enemy radio
A machine that erased memories
Harsh treatment, hunger and pressure
check.why: The reading says later research found harsh treatment, hunger and pressure explained most of it, not a magic method.

lessons.title: What MKUltra Paid For
lessons.mainIdea: MKUltra secretly paid outside researchers to study drugs, hypnosis and other ways to change how people think and act.
reading: MKUltra was run by the CIA's Technical Services staff. Its best-known leader was Sidney Gottlieb, a chemist. The program did not build one big laboratory. Instead, it paid outside researchers at universities, hospitals, prisons and private companies. Those projects were called *subprojects*. Investigators later counted about 150 of them.

Many researchers did not know the CIA was paying them. The money often passed through a *front organization*, a group that looks independent but secretly serves someone else. A foundation with a scientific-sounding name could hand out grants while hiding where the money came from.

The subprojects studied many things. Some tested LSD, a powerful drug that changes perception, mood and thinking. Some studied hypnosis, sleep, stress and ways to get information from people during questioning, called *interrogation*. Some were ordinary science that simply had a secret sponsor. Others crossed clear lines, as the next lesson shows.

Because the program was spread across so many places and hidden behind other names, it was hard to see from the outside. That same spread later helped investigators. Each subproject left payment records behind. Money records name who was paid, when, and for what. They are hard to hide completely.

words.d: the separate research jobs that MKUltra paid for, each with its own number and budget
a group that looks independent but secretly works for, or is paid by, someone else
formal questioning of a person to get information, often by police, soldiers or spies

look.title: Following a Grant
look.text: A psychology professor receives a grant from a foundation. The foundation's letterhead lists doctors and scientists. The professor studies how stress affects memory and publishes the results. Twenty years later, a Senate report shows the foundation's money came from the CIA.
look.prompt: Did the professor do anything wrong? What would you want to know before you decide?

check.q: What is a front organization?
choices: A CIA office in a foreign country
A group that looks independent but secretly serves someone else
The first team to test a new drug
A Senate committee that reviews spy agencies
check.why: A front organization hides who is really behind it; MKUltra used them so researchers did not see the CIA's name.

check.q: About how many MKUltra subprojects did investigators later count?
choices: About 15
About 1,500
About 15,000
About 150
check.why: The reading says investigators later counted about 150 subprojects.

check.q: Why did MKUltra's spread across many places later help investigators?
choices: Each subproject left payment records behind
Every researcher kept a diary of the program
The universities published all the results
The CIA posted a list on its website
check.why: Each subproject was paid for, so its money trail left records that could be found later.

lessons.title: Consent and the Unwitting
lessons.mainIdea: The worst harm in MKUltra came from testing drugs on people who did not know and had not agreed.
reading: After World War II, judges at Nuremberg, Germany, tried Nazi doctors who had done cruel experiments on prisoners. In 1947 the court set out rules for research on people. These rules are called the Nuremberg Code. The first rule is about *informed consent*. That means a person agrees to take part, freely, after being told what will happen and what the risks are.

MKUltra broke that rule in some of its work. The CIA wanted to know how drugs would affect people who did not expect them, as an enemy's victim would not expect them. So some people were given LSD without being told. The word for such people is *unwitting*: they did not know. Records show tests on unwitting people in ordinary places, including a CIA-run apartment in San Francisco.

Other subjects were patients, prisoners or people with addictions. They might have signed a form, but they had little real choice or little real information. Researchers call such people *vulnerable*: their situation makes it hard to say no or to understand the risk.

Not every MKUltra subproject harmed anyone. But the unwitting tests are why the program became a lasting symbol. They show what can happen when secrecy removes the usual checks on research. Rules like informed consent exist so that no one, not even a government agency, can decide alone that a person's body may be used for a test.

words.d: freely agreeing to take part in something after being told clearly what will happen and what the risks are
not knowing; an unwitting test subject does not know they are part of an experiment
in a situation that makes it hard to refuse, to understand a risk, or to protect oneself
rules for research on human beings, set out in 1947 by the court that tried Nazi doctors

look.title: The First Rule of the Nuremberg Code
look.text: The voluntary consent of the person being studied is absolutely essential. The person must be legally able to consent, free to choose without force or trickery, and must understand enough about the experiment to make an informed decision.
look.cite: The Nuremberg Code, Principle 1, from the judgment in United States v. Karl Brandt et al., Nuremberg Military Tribunal, 1947 (paraphrase)
look.prompt: Name two parts of this rule that an unwitting MKUltra test broke. Use the words of the rule.

check.q: What does 'informed consent' mean?
choices: Agreeing freely after being told what will happen and the risks
Being paid well for taking part in a study
Getting permission from a government agency
Signing any form that a researcher hands you
check.why: Informed consent means freely agreeing after a clear explanation of what will happen and the risks.

check.q: Why did the CIA give LSD to some people without telling them?
choices: The drug was legal and considered harmless
The people had asked to try it
It wanted to see how drugs affect people who do not expect them
The Nuremberg Code allowed it in wartime
check.why: The CIA wanted to learn how an unexpected drug would affect a person, so it tested some people who did not know.

check.q: Which person best fits the word 'vulnerable' as the reading uses it?
choices: A senator who questions a CIA director
A reporter who asks for records
A foundation that hands out grants
A prisoner who signs a form but has little real choice
check.why: The reading calls patients, prisoners and people with addictions vulnerable because their situation makes refusing hard.

lessons.title: A Drink at a Retreat
lessons.mainIdea: In November 1953, Army scientist Frank Olson was secretly given LSD, and nine days later he died after a fall from a New York hotel window.
reading: Frank Olson was a scientist who worked for the U.S. Army at Camp Detrick in Maryland, studying germs that could be used as weapons. He had a wife and three children. In November 1953, he went to a work retreat at Deep Creek Lake in western Maryland with Army and CIA colleagues.

At the retreat, CIA officers from Sidney Gottlieb's group put LSD into a drink and gave it to several of the men. Olson did not know. In the days that followed, he became deeply troubled and anxious. His colleagues took him to New York City to see a doctor who worked with the CIA.

Early on 28 November 1953, Olson fell from a tenth-floor window of the Statler Hotel in New York and died. For more than twenty years, his family was told only that he had suffered a breakdown. They were not told about the LSD. His death was treated as a private tragedy, not as the result of a secret *experiment*.

Olson's story matters because it puts a face on the word unwitting. He was a trained scientist and a government employee. He still had no chance to say no. His family would not learn the truth for more than twenty years. The next lesson tells how they found out.

words.d: a test done to find out what happens under certain conditions
the U.S. Army research base in Frederick, Maryland, where Frank Olson worked
a meeting held away from the usual workplace, often for several days

look.title: What the Family Was Told
look.text: For 22 years, the Olson children grew up believing their father had an emotional breakdown for no clear reason. No one told them about the drink at Deep Creek Lake. The people who knew worked for the government that employed him.
look.prompt: How can a secret kept by an institution affect a family long after the event itself? Give one specific way.

check.q: Where did CIA officers secretly give Frank Olson LSD?
choices: At the Statler Hotel in New York
At a work retreat at Deep Creek Lake, Maryland
At CIA headquarters in Virginia
At a Senate hearing room
check.why: The drug was put into a drink at the Deep Creek Lake retreat in November 1953.

check.q: When did Frank Olson die?
choices: 13 April 1953
3 August 1977
28 November 1953
January 1973
check.why: Olson died early on 28 November 1953, after the fall in New York.

check.q: What was Olson's family told for more than twenty years?
choices: That he had been poisoned by a foreign spy
That he had died in a car accident
That he had been given LSD in a test
That he had suffered a breakdown
check.why: The family was told only of a breakdown; the LSD was kept from them until 1975.

lessons.title: The Truth Comes Out in 1975
lessons.mainIdea: Olson's family learned about the LSD in 1975, received an apology from President Ford, and still disputes how he died.
reading: In June 1975, a presidential commission released a report on CIA activities inside the United States. One passage described an Army employee who had been given LSD without his knowledge in 1953 and who died days later after jumping or falling from a hotel window. The report did not give his name. The Olson family read it and recognized their father.

The family spoke publicly. In July 1975, President Gerald Ford met them at the White House and apologized on behalf of the government. Congress later approved a payment to the family. For the first time, the government admitted in public that one of its own secret tests had led to a death.

The story did not end there. Olson's sons came to believe the official account was still incomplete. In the 1990s they had his body examined again. They argue that he did not jump but was killed to keep secrets. Others hold that the drug and his distress explain the fall. No court or official inquiry has settled this *dispute*.

So there are two kinds of fact here. It is *documented* that Olson was secretly drugged and died days later. How exactly he died remains contested. Keeping those two kinds of fact apart is one of the most useful habits a reader of history can build. Both matter.

words.d: a group appointed to study a problem and report on it
a disagreement that has not been settled
shown by records made at the time or by official findings, not just by memory or rumor

look.title: The Report That Did Not Name Him
look.text: The commission reported that in 1953 an employee of the Department of the Army was given LSD without his knowledge as part of a CIA test. Soon afterward he showed serious emotional distress, and within days he died after jumping from a tenth-floor hotel window in New York.
look.cite: Report to the President by the Commission on CIA Activities within the United States (Rockefeller Commission), June 1975 (paraphrase)
look.prompt: The report does not name Olson. How could his family still tell it was about him? What does leaving out the name suggest?

check.q: How did the Olson family first learn about the LSD?
choices: From a 1975 government report that described the case without his name
From a letter Frank Olson left behind
From a newspaper story in 1953
From the 1977 Senate hearing
check.why: The Rockefeller Commission report of June 1975 described the case, and the family recognized it.

check.q: What did President Ford do in July 1975?
choices: He ordered the MKUltra files destroyed
He created the Church Committee
He met the Olson family and apologized
He testified before the Senate
check.why: Ford met the family at the White House and apologized on behalf of the government.

check.q: Which part of Olson's story is still disputed?
choices: Whether he worked for the Army
Whether he was given LSD without knowing
Whether he died in 1953
Exactly how he came to fall from the window
check.why: The drugging and his death are documented; his sons argue he was killed, and no inquiry has settled how he died.

lessons.title: The Order of 1973
lessons.mainIdea: In January 1973, CIA Director Richard Helms ordered MKUltra's files destroyed, which is why much of the program can never be fully known.
reading: In January 1973, Richard Helms was leaving his job as director of the CIA. Before he left, he ordered MKUltra's files destroyed. Sidney Gottlieb, who was retiring too, carried out the order. Most of the program's working papers and reports were destroyed.

The timing matters. The Watergate scandal was growing in Washington. Congress and reporters were starting to ask hard questions about what the government had done in secret. Records that were destroyed could not be demanded later. Helms and Gottlieb later gave reasons, such as protecting the privacy of the researchers and subjects. Critics saw a simpler motive: removing the evidence.

Historians call the destruction of records a *gap in the record*. It is a real hole, not a sign of anything in particular. A gap tells you that something was there. It does not tell you what was there. That difference is important for the rest of this chapter.

Destroying records is also a kind of evidence in itself. The order shows that leaders knew the files could cause trouble if the public saw them. The 1973 order shows intent to hide. It does not tell us exactly what the lost pages said. Hiding and proving are different things.

words.d: a part of history where the evidence is missing, lost or destroyed
the early-1970s political scandal over a break-in and cover-up that led President Nixon to resign in 1974
the reason a person does something

look.title: From Approval to Hearing
look.cite: Rockefeller Commission (1975); Church Committee Final Report (1976); U.S. Senate joint hearing on Project MKULTRA (1977)
look.prompt: How many years passed between the destruction order and the Senate hearing? What had changed in the country in between?

check.q: Who ordered the MKUltra files destroyed in January 1973?
choices: Allen Dulles
Richard Helms
Stansfield Turner
Gerald Ford
check.why: Richard Helms, as he was leaving the job of CIA director, ordered the files destroyed.

check.q: What does a 'gap in the record' tell a historian?
choices: That something was there, but not what it was
Exactly what the missing files said
That the event never happened
That the missing papers were harmless
check.why: The reading says a gap shows something was there but does not tell you what was there.

check.q: Why does the timing of the 1973 order matter?
choices: It came right after MKUltra was approved
It came after the Church Committee had finished
It came as Watergate made Congress and reporters ask hard questions
It came after the files had been found in 1977
check.why: The order came while the Watergate scandal was growing and people were starting to question government secrets.

lessons.title: Saved by the Accountants
lessons.mainIdea: About 20,000 documents of MKUltra records survived because they were filed with financial records rather than with the program's main files.
reading: Helms's order reached the program's main files. It did not reach every piece of paper MKUltra had created. Money leaves a trail. Each subproject needed contracts, invoices and payment approvals. Those were handled by the CIA's finance staff and stored in a different place, among retired *financial records*.

In 1977, a search for records turned up these files. The search followed a Freedom of Information Act request from writer John Marks. The *Freedom of Information Act*, passed in 1966 and strengthened in 1974, lets anyone ask a federal agency for its records. The agency must search and must explain what it holds back.

The surviving papers came to about 20,000 documents. They did not contain the full research reports. They did show who was paid, how much, for which subproject, and often a short description of the work. That was enough to identify many universities, hospitals and researchers.

The lesson is practical. When you look for evidence of a hidden program, look where money moved. Budgets, receipts and payroll are dull, but they are hard to erase, because many different offices keep copies. Many copies in many hands make a secret much harder to erase.

words.d: papers that track money, such as contracts, invoices, receipts and payments
a 1966 U.S. law that lets anyone request records from federal agencies; often called FOIA
a bill that lists what was provided and how much is owed

look.title: Where Would You Look?
look.text: Imagine a school club spent money on a trip, and later someone threw away the trip's sign-up sheets and photos. The club treasurer still has the bank statements. The bus company still has its bill. The school office still has the permission forms.
look.prompt: List three things the surviving papers could prove about the trip and one thing they could not prove. Then connect your answer to the MKUltra financial files.

check.q: Why did about 20,000 documents of MKUltra records survive?
choices: They were filed with financial records, apart from the main files
Helms decided to keep a secret copy
A senator hid them in his office
They were printed in a newspaper in 1973
check.why: The payment records were stored separately among retired financial files, which the destruction order missed.

check.q: What does the Freedom of Information Act allow?
choices: Anyone to join a Senate committee
The CIA to destroy old records
Anyone to ask a federal agency for its records
Reporters to arrest government officials
check.why: FOIA lets anyone request federal agency records, and the agency must search.

check.q: What did the surviving papers mostly show?
choices: The full results of every experiment
The names of every unwitting subject
Proof that mind control worked
Who was paid, how much, and for which subproject
check.why: They were financial records, so they showed payments and short descriptions, not full research reports.

lessons.title: The Hearing of 3 August 1977
lessons.mainIdea: At a joint Senate hearing on 3 August 1977, CIA Director Stansfield Turner told senators what the recovered MKUltra records showed.
reading: On 3 August 1977, two Senate groups met together: the new Select Committee on Intelligence and the Subcommittee on Health and Scientific Research, led by Senator Edward Kennedy. The witness was Admiral Stansfield Turner, whom President Jimmy Carter had made CIA director that year.

Turner did not defend the program. He told the senators that the recovered papers had been found in financial files and described what they covered: drug tests, including on unwitting people, research on behavior, and funding hidden through outside groups. He said the CIA would try to identify the institutions involved and let them know.

A *hearing* is a meeting where lawmakers question witnesses in public or in private and create an official record. This one was printed as a government document. It became one of the main *primary sources* on MKUltra. A primary source is a record made at the time by people involved in the events.

The hearing also showed a new kind of relationship. A CIA director was answering questions from a permanent committee whose job was to watch his agency. Before 1976, no such Senate committee had existed. The hearing itself was a sign that the rules had changed.

words.d: a meeting where lawmakers question witnesses and make an official record
a record made at the time by people involved in the events, such as a letter, report or transcript
a person who gives information, often under oath, to a court or committee

look.title: What the Director Told the Senate
look.text: The CIA director explained that a new search had turned up MKUltra papers in retired financial files. He said they described tests of drugs on people, some of whom did not know, and research paid for through outside organizations. He said the agency would try to notify the institutions involved.
look.cite: U.S. Senate, Select Committee on Intelligence and Subcommittee on Health and Scientific Research, Project MKULTRA, joint hearing, 3 August 1977 (paraphrase)
look.prompt: Why is a hearing transcript like this stronger evidence than a later magazine article about MKUltra? Give one reason.

check.q: Who testified about the recovered MKUltra records on 3 August 1977?
choices: Richard Helms
Sidney Gottlieb
Stansfield Turner
Nelson Rockefeller
check.why: CIA Director Admiral Stansfield Turner was the witness at the joint Senate hearing.

check.q: Which senator led the health subcommittee that joined the hearing?
choices: Edward Kennedy
Frank Church
Allen Dulles
John Marks
check.why: Senator Edward Kennedy led the Subcommittee on Health and Scientific Research.

check.q: Why is the printed hearing a primary source?
choices: It was written by a historian decades later
It was made at the time by people involved in the events
It was approved by a newspaper editor
It contains no mistakes at all
check.why: A primary source is made at the time by people involved; the hearing record fits that definition.

lessons.title: A Story and a Commission
lessons.mainIdea: A December 1974 newspaper story about CIA spying at home led President Ford to appoint the Rockefeller Commission in January 1975.
reading: In December 1974, reporter Seymour Hersh wrote in The New York Times that the CIA had spied on thousands of Americans inside the United States, mostly people who opposed the Vietnam War. The CIA's charter was meant to keep it focused on other countries, not on Americans at home. The story caused an uproar.

In January 1975, President Gerald Ford named a commission to look into it. Vice President Nelson Rockefeller led it, so it is called the *Rockefeller Commission*. Its report came out in June 1975. It confirmed a CIA program, called Operation CHAOS, that had gathered files on American protesters. It also described drug testing, including the case that turned out to be Frank Olson's.

Critics said the commission was too close to the government it was studying. Several members were former officials. It worked for only a few months. Supporters said it still put key facts on the public record for the first time. Commissions like this are one way a president can answer public worry.

Notice the chain. A reporter's story led to a commission. The commission's report led a family to the truth. Each step made the next one possible. This is how *accountability* often works: in steps, not all at once. A single story rarely tells the whole truth, but it can start the search.

words.d: the group led by Vice President Nelson Rockefeller that investigated CIA activities inside the U.S. in 1975
being required to explain your actions and accept the consequences
the official document or law that says what an organization is for and what it may do

look.title: Too Close to Judge?
look.text: A school board asks three former principals to investigate complaints about the principal's office. Parents worry the former principals will go easy on their old colleagues. The board says they know how a school works and will find the facts faster.
look.prompt: How is this like the criticism of the Rockefeller Commission? What would make an investigation more trusted?

check.q: What set off the 1975 investigations of the CIA?
choices: A 1974 New York Times story by Seymour Hersh
The 1977 Senate hearing
A letter from the Olson family
The FBI break-in at Media, Pennsylvania
check.why: Hersh's December 1974 story on CIA spying at home led to the Rockefeller Commission and more.

check.q: What was Operation CHAOS?
choices: The MKUltra drug-testing program
A plan to invade Cuba
A CIA program that gathered files on American protesters
A Senate rule on spy agencies
check.why: The Rockefeller Commission confirmed that Operation CHAOS kept files on American protesters.

check.q: What did critics say about the Rockefeller Commission?
choices: It had no members from government
It worked for more than ten years
It named every MKUltra subject
It was too close to the government it was studying
check.why: Critics noted several members were former officials and that it worked only a few months.

lessons.title: The Church Committee
lessons.mainIdea: The Senate's Church Committee (1975–1976) studied the CIA, FBI and other agencies and published the fullest public account of their secret abuses.
reading: On 27 January 1975, the Senate created a special committee to study the government's intelligence agencies. Its chairman was Senator Frank Church of Idaho, so it is known as the *Church Committee*. The House of Representatives set up its own inquiry, called the Pike Committee.

The Church Committee had staff, a budget and the power to demand documents and question witnesses under *subpoena*, a legal order to appear or to hand over records. It looked at the CIA, the FBI, the National Security Agency and others. It held public hearings and many private ones.

Its final report was issued on 29 April 1976, in six books totaling about 2,700 pages. It covered MKUltra and other drug testing, CIA plots against foreign leaders, and the FBI's secret campaign against American groups, which the next chapter explores.

The committee's members did not all agree. Some worried that revealing secrets could hurt the country or put agents at risk. Others said that hidden abuses were the greater danger to a free country. That debate, between *secrecy* and oversight, has never fully ended.

words.d: the U.S. Senate committee, led by Senator Frank Church, that investigated intelligence agencies in 1975–1976
a legal order that requires a person to appear and testify or to hand over records
keeping information hidden from others on purpose
watching over and reviewing the work of an agency to make sure it follows the law

look.title: The Committee's Warning
look.text: The committee concluded that intelligence agencies had too often acted outside the law and beyond public view. It warned that secret power used against citizens, even for goals that seemed good, threatens the freedoms the agencies were meant to protect.
look.cite: U.S. Senate Select Committee to Study Governmental Operations with Respect to Intelligence Activities (Church Committee), Final Report, Book II, 1976 (paraphrase)
look.prompt: The committee says good goals do not make secret power safe. Find one example from this chapter that supports its warning.

check.q: Who was the chairman of the Church Committee?
choices: Senator Edward Kennedy
Vice President Nelson Rockefeller
Senator Frank Church
President Jimmy Carter
check.why: Senator Frank Church of Idaho chaired the committee, which is why it carries his name.

check.q: What is a subpoena?
choices: A legal order to appear or hand over records
A secret CIA test
A kind of newspaper story
A vote to end a committee
check.why: A subpoena legally requires a person to testify or produce records, which gave the committee real power.

check.q: When was the Church Committee's final report issued?
choices: December 1974
January 1973
3 August 1977
29 April 1976
check.why: The final report came out on 29 April 1976, in six books.

lessons.title: Proven and Not Proven
lessons.mainIdea: The records prove that MKUltra drugged unwitting people and hid its funding, but they do not prove that it achieved real mind control.
reading: Because MKUltra was real and hidden, it has become the base for many larger stories. A careful reader sorts the claims into three groups. First, what is *documented*: the program existed from 1953; it paid about 150 subprojects; it tested drugs on some people without their knowledge; Frank Olson was drugged and died; most files were destroyed in 1973.

Second, what is *contested*: how Olson died; how many people were harmed in total; exactly what some subprojects did. Honest researchers disagree, because the evidence is incomplete. In Canada, patients at a Montreal psychiatric hospital who went through harsh treatments in work partly paid for by MKUltra later sued, and some won settlements.

Third, what is *not supported* by the records: that MKUltra built a working method to control people's minds, or that it created programmed assassins. Investigators found no evidence of this. Many who worked on the program said the results were disappointing.

The destroyed files leave real gaps. Some people fill those gaps with the most dramatic answer. Historians leave a gap as a gap and say what is and is not known. Saying "we do not know" is honest. It is also a strong position when others claim to know more than the records show.

words.d: argued over by people who look at the evidence and reach different conclusions
an agreement to end a lawsuit, often with a payment, without a final court ruling
a statement that something is true, which may or may not be backed by evidence

look.title: Sort the Claims
look.text: Claim 1: The CIA gave LSD to some people who did not know it. Claim 2: MKUltra created a secret army of hypnotized assassins. Claim 3: We will never know everything MKUltra did. Claim 4: Frank Olson was murdered to protect secrets.
look.prompt: Label each claim documented, contested or not supported. Name the evidence, or the missing evidence, for each one.

check.q: Which statement about MKUltra is documented?
choices: It created programmed assassins
It tested drugs on some people without their knowledge
It built a working mind-control method
All its records survive today
check.why: Unwitting drug testing is documented in the hearing and the committee reports; the other claims are not.

check.q: Why do honest researchers still disagree about parts of MKUltra?
choices: Because most files were destroyed and the evidence is incomplete
Because the program never existed
Because the Senate never studied it
Because the CIA published everything
check.why: The 1973 destruction left gaps, so some questions cannot be settled from the records.

check.q: According to the reading, what do historians do with a gap in the evidence?
choices: Fill it with the most dramatic answer
Assume nothing happened there
Ask the CIA to fill it in
Leave it as a gap and say what is and is not known
check.why: The reading says historians leave a gap as a gap rather than filling it with a guess.

lessons.title: How Oversight Changed
lessons.mainIdea: After 1975, Congress built permanent intelligence committees and new laws so that secret agencies would answer to elected officials.
reading: The investigations did more than tell stories. They changed how the government works. In May 1976, the Senate created a permanent Select Committee on Intelligence. In 1977, the House created its own permanent intelligence committee. Agencies now had to report to these committees on a regular basis.

In 1976, President Ford issued an executive order that banned U.S. government employees from taking part in political assassination. In 1978, Congress passed the *Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act*, known as FISA. It requires the government to get approval from a special court before it listens in on people inside the United States for intelligence purposes.

Research rules changed too. In the 1970s, federal rules required review boards to approve research on human beings before it starts. These boards check for informed consent. The shock of cases like MKUltra helped push those protections forward. Consent became a rule to check, not a favor to ask.

Oversight is not a machine that runs itself. It depends on members of Congress asking hard questions, on judges, on reporters and on people inside agencies who speak up. The system of the 1970s made abuse harder to hide. It did not make it impossible.

words.d: a 1978 U.S. law requiring approval from a special court before certain spying inside the United States; known as FISA
a written order from the president that directs how the executive branch operates
close watching of a person or group, such as listening to calls or following movements

look.title: What FISA Requires
look.text: Before the government may carry out electronic surveillance inside the United States to gather foreign intelligence, it must, with limited exceptions, ask a special court for an order. The request must explain who is to be watched and why.
look.cite: Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978, Public Law 95-511 (paraphrase)
look.prompt: How does requiring a court's approval change who gets to decide whether someone is watched? Why might Congress have wanted that after the 1970s investigations?

check.q: What did the Senate create in May 1976?
choices: The Rockefeller Commission
A permanent Select Committee on Intelligence
The Freedom of Information Act
The Nuremberg Code
check.why: In May 1976 the Senate made intelligence oversight permanent with the Select Committee on Intelligence.

check.q: What does FISA require?
choices: That all CIA files be made public
That the CIA destroy old records
That the FBI stop all investigations
Approval from a special court before certain spying inside the U.S.
check.why: FISA (1978) requires a special court's order for most intelligence surveillance inside the United States.

check.q: According to the reading, what does oversight depend on?
choices: People such as lawmakers, judges, reporters and insiders who ask and speak up
One law that runs by itself
The CIA director alone
Keeping all records secret
check.why: The reading says oversight is not automatic; it depends on people asking hard questions and speaking up.

review.q: In what year did CIA Director Allen Dulles approve MKUltra?
review.why: Dulles approved MKUltra on 13 April 1953, early in the Cold War.

review.q: Which idea best describes the main ethical problem with MKUltra's unwitting tests?
choices: They cost too much money
They were done outside the United States
They broke the rule of informed consent
They were never written down
review.why: Giving drugs to people who did not know broke informed consent, the first rule of the Nuremberg Code.

review.q: What is documented about Frank Olson?
choices: He was secretly given LSD and died days later in a fall from a hotel window
He led the MKUltra program
He testified at the 1977 hearing
He ordered the files destroyed
review.why: The Rockefeller report and later records show Olson was secretly drugged in 1953 and died nine days later.

review.q: Why can historians never know everything MKUltra did?
choices: The program was only a rumor
The records were written in code
The Senate kept the files sealed
Richard Helms ordered most files destroyed in 1973
review.why: Helms's 1973 order destroyed most working files, leaving a permanent gap in the record.

review.q: How did about 20,000 documents of MKUltra records survive?
choices: A reporter stole them in 1971
They were stored with financial records the destruction order missed
Gottlieb kept copies at home
They were sent to a foreign government
review.why: The payment records were filed separately and were found in 1977 during a FOIA search.

review.q: How did the Rockefeller Commission differ from the Church Committee?
choices: The commission was appointed by the president; the committee was created by the Senate
The commission studied the FBI only; the committee studied the CIA only
The commission came after 1977; the committee came before 1970
The commission had subpoena power; the committee had none
review.why: President Ford appointed the Rockefeller Commission; the Senate created the Church Committee in January 1975.

review.q: Which claim about MKUltra is NOT supported by the records?
choices: It funded research through front organizations
It tested LSD on some unwitting people
It produced a working method of mind control
Its main files were destroyed in 1973
review.why: Investigators found no evidence of working mind control; the other three are documented.

review.q: Which change came out of the 1970s investigations?
choices: The CIA was closed
The Cold War ended
The Freedom of Information Act was first created
Congress created permanent intelligence committees and passed FISA
review.why: The Senate (1976) and House (1977) created permanent committees, and FISA passed in 1978.
